content: The Guideline Development Group (GDG) was required to complete the standard World Health Organization (WHO) Declaration of Interest (DOI) forms. These forms were subsequently reviewed. The WHO Secretariat conducted a thorough review of the curriculum vitae of each potential participant and performed internet searches using platforms such as PubMed, Open Payments Data, and Google Scholar to identify any potential financial or academic conflicts of interest related to the subject matter of the meeting. All DOI forms are securely stored at the WHO Department of Noncommunicable Diseases. The WHO Steering Group made the names and brief biographies of potential GDG members publicly available on the WHO website for over two weeks. This was accompanied by a description of the meeting's objectives to allow for public review and comment. No concerns were raised regarding any of the members. None of the declared interests were deemed significant enough to compromise the objectivity of the experts' judgments during the guideline development process or the recommendations. Consequently, no member was excluded from full participation in the guideline development process. During the guideline development process, one GDG member's conflict of interest status changed when she accepted a temporary appointment as a staff member at WHO. Upon accepting this appointment, she was immediately removed from further GDG engagements. All GDG members and meeting observers were required to sign a confidentiality agreement before participating in the meeting. Members of the External Review Group (ERG) were also required to complete the standard WHO DOI forms, which were reviewed. None of the declared interests were considered significant enough to affect the judgment of the reviewers or to exclude their participation as expert reviewers. The WHO Steering Group, in consultation with the GDG and methodologists, developed a list of treatment outcomes most relevant to the care of individuals with hypertension. The GDG rated each outcome on a scale from 1 to 9, categorizing them as critical (rated 7–9), important (rated 4–6), or not important (rated 1–3) for decision-making purposes. The systematic reviews were guided by 11 PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcomes) questions. These questions addressed key aspects of hypertension management, including: 1. The blood pressure thresholds at which pharmacological therapy should be initiated to prevent cardiovascular events. 2. The necessity of laboratory testing prior to or during the titration of antihypertensive treatments. 3. The role of cardiovascular risk assessment in guiding the initiation of antihypertensive medications. 4. The selection of first-line pharmacological agents for adults with hypertension. 5. The comparative effectiveness of different first-line antihypertensive drugs in head-to-head studies. 6. The use of monotherapy versus combination therapy as first-line treatment for hypertension. 7. The optimal combination therapy of two or more antihypertensive drugs. 8. The potential benefits of single-pill combinations of antihypertensive drugs in improving outcomes. 9. The target blood pressure levels that pharmacological treatment should aim to achieve. 10. The appropriate intervals for reassessing blood pressure in patients receiving pharmacological treatment. 11. The feasibility of providing pharmacological management of hypertension by nonphysician care providers. Each PICO question was designed to evaluate specific outcomes, including all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, stroke, myocardial infarction, end-stage renal disease, heart failure events, cognitive impairment or dementia, adverse effects, blood pressure control, patient satisfaction, and adherence. The analyses also considered various effect modifiers, such as estimated cardiovascular risk, pre-existing conditions (e.g., coronary artery disease, stroke, diabetes), age, sex, chronic kidney disease, race/ethnicity, and baseline blood pressure levels.
